newsitem.title: FRANCE: Corsican bombers hit French mainland targets.
newsitem.headline: Corsican bombers hit French mainland targets.

text.p: Corsican separatists claimed responsibility on Thursday for two bombings in the southern French city of Nimes, defying a promised government crackdown after two earlier attacks on France's mainland.

A caller told a local television station that the outlawed Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC) planted bombs overnight which caused damage but no casualties at a tax office and courthouse in Nimes.
Two other bombs exploded in Corsica, hours after a leading nationalist was sentenced to a prison term after being convicted in his absence for carrying guns.
One hit a courthouse in l'Ile Rousse, a town of which Veterans Affairs Minister Pierre Pasquini is mayor, and another exploded at a discotheque in Ajaccio, the French Mediterranean island's capital.
Both did extensive damage but injured no one.
On Wednesday, an appeals court in Bastia sentenced the leader of the most militant separatist group, Francois Santoni, in his absence to four months in jail, with another eight months suspended.

Santoni, 36, secretary-general of A Cuncolta Naziunalista, the legal front for the FLNC's Historical Wing, is in hiding and said to be under heavy armed guard. He escaped unharmed from an attempt on his life in May, 1995.
In an apparent act of retaliation, an unknown attacker threw an incendiary device into the entrance of the Bastia courthouse on Thursday, but caused no damage.
In Paris, the pool of anti-terrorism magistrates launched investigations into all four bombings, taking to 50 or so the number of probes under way into Corsican attacks.

It also opened a probe into a clandestine January 11 news conference in the central hills of Corsica at which some 600 hooded guerrillas called a three-month truce, staging a show of force on the eve of a visit by Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre.

Many of the guerrillas carried rocket-propelled grenades, assault rifles and machine pistols. Critics derided security forces at the time for arresting no one and only taking down the car number plates.

The FLNC "truce", breached by dozens of bombings on the island, expired last Saturday, a week after the movement planted a bomb at Prime Minister Alain Juppe's mayoral office in the southwestern French city of Bordeaux.
In late September, the FLNC's Historical Wing had claimed responsibility for the bombing of the lawcourts in Aix-en-Provence in southern France.

Juppe responded by vowing to crack down on separatist gunmen and put "Corsican terrorism" out of action. Guerrillas targeted the law courts in Aix-en-Provence in early September, the first mainland bombing in several years.
Although street patrols, random roadblocks and guards on public buildings have been increased, there has so far been no roundup of known militants.

The magazine Paris-Match ran an interview on Thursday with a man describing himself as a spokesman for the FLNC's Historical Wing and demanding President Jacques Chirac take concrete steps to enable talks to restart and the bombings to stop.

The unnamed interviewee demanded that Corsica be given the status of a French overseas territory "implying the recognition of the Corsican people". Corsicans would then decide whether the island should be granted independence.
